title: Strengths & limitations of each life cycle
blurb: Weigh the strengths and limitations of linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles, and explain how a project manager reduces each limitation.
question: A logistics company is running two projects: a new warehouse built to a fixed design and a driver app that will evolve with drivers' feedback. The board asks the project manager to explain the strengths and limitations of the life cycle chosen for each. What should the answer cover?

teach.h: Every life cycle is a trade-off
teach.body: No life cycle is good at everything. A linear life cycle buys predictability and control at the price of flexibility and late feedback. An iterative life cycle buys flexibility and early value at the price of certainty about the final scope. A hybrid tries to get the best of both, at the price of extra complexity. In plain English: knowing what each model is weak at tells you what to watch for, and how to protect the project against it.

teach.h: Strengths and limitations at a glance

Adapts to change; users involved throughout
Early feedback reduces the risk of building the wrong thing
Final scope uncertain; total hard to forecast
Needs committed users and a product owner
Harder to contract; can drift without discipline

teach.body: The warehouse runs linear. Strengths: a fixed-price construction contract, a clear baseline and confident reporting to the board. Limitation: when the operations team asked for different racking during Deployment, it meant costly rework. The driver app runs iterative. Strengths: route planning went live in month two and drivers' feedback improved every release. Limitation: when the product owner was pulled onto other work for three weeks, priorities drifted and the team built low-value features.

teach.text: Don't swap the strengths. Predictability, a clear baseline and easy contracting belong to LINEAR. Early value, adaptability and early feedback belong to ITERATIVE. And don't overstate the weaknesses: iterative does not mean 'no planning, no governance, no documentation', and linear does not mean 'no change allowed'; linear handles change through formal change control.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Give at least two strengths and two limitations for each life cycle the question names.
Explain each point, don't just list it: say WHY it is a strength or a limitation.
Link each point to the scenario (for example, a fixed-price contract or users who keep changing their minds).
Where asked, add a mitigation for each limitation.
Finish by saying which life cycle fits the scenario best, and why.
Linear: predictable, controlled, easy to contract; but inflexible, late feedback, costly late change, late benefits.
Iterative: early value, adaptable, user-involved, risk reduced by feedback; but uncertain final scope, needs committed users, harder to contract, can drift.
Hybrid: the best of both; but complex, with interfaces and governance to align.
Each limitation has a typical mitigation a project manager can apply.
Strengths and limitations are why the choice of life cycle depends on the project.

summary: You can now weigh the strengths and limitations of linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles. You can also explain how a project manager reduces each limitation and use these trade-offs to justify a choice in a written answer.

A.q: Which is a key strength of a linear life cycle?
options: Scope that flexes as users learn
A clear baseline that aids control
A.why: Linear sets a full baseline in Definition, giving predictability and strong control of time, cost and scope.

whyNot.0: Early value from releases is an iterative strength.
whyNot.1: Flexing scope is an iterative feature.
whyNot.3: Frequent user feedback is an iterative strength.

A.q: Which is a typical limitation of an iterative life cycle?
options: The final scope is hard to forecast
Users see nothing until the end
It needs a full specification first
A.why: Because scope flexes and emerges, it is hard to say up front exactly what the final solution will contain.

whyNot.1: Users seeing nothing until the end is a LINEAR limitation.
whyNot.2: Costly late change is a LINEAR limitation; iterative expects change.
whyNot.3: A full up-front specification is a linear feature, not an iterative need.

A.q: Which is the main limitation of a hybrid life cycle?
A.why: Running two approaches in one project creates interfaces, dependencies and governance that must be aligned.

whyNot.0: Hybrid is used widely, for example building works alongside software.
whyNot.1: Hybrid often borrows decision gates from linear.
whyNot.2: Hybrid keeps flexibility in its iterative parts.

B.q: A linear office refurbishment reaches Deployment before staff see the new layout, and they dislike it. Which limitation of linear does this illustrate?
B.why: In linear projects users often give real feedback only once outputs exist, when changes are expensive.

whyNot.0: Gates are control points; they didn't cause the late feedback.
whyNot.2: Linear scope is fixed in a baseline; it doesn't flex easily.
whyNot.3: Linear sets a baseline in Definition; this one had one.

B.q: Why is it often harder to agree a fixed-price contract for an iterative project?
options: Suppliers can't work in time boxes
Fixed prices are banned in agile
The full scope isn't known first
B.why: A fixed price needs a well-defined scope. In iterative working the scope emerges, so a fixed price for a fixed scope is hard to agree.

whyNot.1: Suppliers commonly work in time boxes.
whyNot.2: Nothing bans fixed prices; it is simply harder to fix scope.

B.q:
Which TWO are strengths of an iterative life cycle?
1) Early delivery of value
2) Predictable total scope
3) Adapts well to change
4) Easy fixed-price contracting
B.why: Early value and adaptability to change are the headline iterative strengths.

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: easy fixed-price contracting is a linear strength.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is wrong: a predictable total scope is a linear strength.
whyNot.3: Both statements are linear strengths, not iterative ones.

C.q: A sponsor needs a firm total cost and end date for a funding bid, and the requirements are well understood. Which strength matters most here?
C.why: A firm cost and date with stable requirements calls for linear's predictability and a full baseline.

whyNot.0: Early value doesn't give the firm total cost the bid needs.
whyNot.1: Adaptability matters little when requirements are well understood.
whyNot.3: Nothing here is uncertain, so hybrid adds complexity for no gain.

C.q: Kestrel's driver-app product owner is rarely available, so priorities drift and the team builds low-value features. Which limitation is shown?
options: It needs a detailed plan up front
It makes late changes very costly
It delivers all benefits at the end
C.why: Iterative working depends on a committed product owner and users to set priorities and give feedback.

whyNot.0: A detailed up-front plan is a linear trait, not this problem.
whyNot.2: Iterative absorbs change through the backlog; cost of change isn't the issue here.
whyNot.3: Iterative delivers benefits incrementally, not all at the end.

C.q: A mostly linear project has a few requirements users find hard to pin down. Which action BEST reduces the related linear limitation?
options: Remove the gates to save time
Fix the scope tighter at Concept
C.why: Prototyping lets users react to the uncertain parts before the baseline is fixed, reducing the risk of late feedback and costly change.

whyNot.0: Removing gates weakens control without addressing late feedback.
whyNot.1: Tightening scope too early locks in the uncertainty.
whyNot.2: Skipping Transition leaves users unprepared and doesn't help requirements.

reteach.title: Organising a music festival
reteach.question: One festival books its whole line-up a year ahead. Another books headliners early but adds acts as ticket sales show what fans want. What does each gain and lose?

blocks.h: Certainty or flexibility: you can't have all of both
blocks.body: The book-everything-early festival knows its costs, can print posters and sells tickets on a fixed line-up: predictable and controlled (linear strengths). But if a genre suddenly takes off, it can't respond (a linear limitation). The add-as-you-go festival can follow what fans want (iterative strengths), but it can't say exactly who is playing, which makes sponsors and budgets harder to pin down (iterative limitations).

blocks.text: The festival that books headliners early and adds the rest later is a hybrid: more control and more flexibility, but more to coordinate.

explain.body: Strengths: a clear plan and baseline, predictability, strong control, easy to contract and report. Limitations: inflexible, late user feedback, costly late change and benefits that arrive only after handover.

test.q: Which is a LIMITATION, not a strength, of a linear life cycle?
test.why: Linear delivers outputs at the end, so benefits usually only begin after handover.

whyNot.1: Easy reporting against a baseline is a linear strength.
whyNot.2: Forecastable costs are a linear strength.
whyNot.3: Simpler fixed contracts are a linear strength.

explain.body: Strengths: early value, adapts to change, users involved throughout, and early feedback reduces the risk of building the wrong thing. Limitations: uncertain final scope, dependence on committed users and a product owner, harder contracting and forecasting, and drift without discipline.

test.q: How does early feedback in an iterative life cycle reduce risk?
options: It fixes the total budget early
It removes the need for testing
test.why: Users see working increments early, so mismatches with their needs are spotted while they are cheap to fix.

whyNot.0: Feedback shapes scope; it doesn't fix the total budget.
whyNot.1: Testing is still needed; feedback complements it.
whyNot.3: Feedback usually changes the scope; that is its purpose.

explain.body: Strength: control and predictability where they matter, flexibility and feedback where they matter. Limitation: more complexity, because the interfaces, dependencies and governance of the two approaches must be carefully aligned.

test.q: What is the main price paid for the benefits of a hybrid life cycle?
test.why: Hybrid gains control and flexibility, but adds complexity at the interfaces and in governance.

whyNot.0: Hybrid keeps control in its linear parts.
whyNot.2: Its iterative parts can deliver value early.
whyNot.3: Its iterative parts involve users closely.

explain.body: Knowing the limitations lets a project manager mitigate them: prototypes for linear's late feedback, change control and contingency for costly change, an empowered product owner and MoSCoW for iterative uncertainty, one governance framework for hybrid.

test.q: An iterative project keeps adding features beyond its vision. Which mitigation fits best?
test.why: Firm MoSCoW prioritisation against a clear vision, within fixed time boxes, stops scope drifting.

whyNot.0: Removing feedback throws away iterative working's main strength.
whyNot.1: Changing contract terms doesn't control what the team builds.
whyNot.2: Extending time boxes breaks the fixed-time discipline and lets drift continue.
